video.title: They Banned My $35K/Month Page So I Started a Business

summary: Host Chris Koerner describes losing a Facebook page that had generated substantial income, then launching Plans of Grandeur by selling previously unpublished creator training to his newsletter. He tests prices and email formats with randomized subscriber groups, takes payment through Stripe, and later organizes the material in a community. He reports that the launch generated tens of thousands of dollars in revenue and profit, while presenting his process as a repeatable way to sell useful content to an existing audience. The video also discusses his former creator consulting, Facebook monetization, newsletter tutorials, and small-list sales of courses and events.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: The Koerner Office host and operator of Plans of Grandeur.

ideas.name: Plans of Grandeur creator training library
ideas.one_liner: Sell a one-time lifetime purchase of unpublished creator training and add future content for buyers.
ideas.business_model: One-off digital product payment, with future training added to the purchased library; 12 AMAs were also promised.
ideas.customer: People who want to grow a personal or business brand, make content, or go viral, including faceless creators.
ideas.problem: Aspiring creators need practical guidance and resources to create content and grow a following or brand.
ideas.offer: Videos, guides, documents, and tracking spreadsheets from Koerner's Google Drive, later organized in a community. Buyers receive future tactical content and 12 recorded AMAs.

pricing.model: One-time lifetime payment; presale price was tested against two price points, then the $97 price was selected. A higher full launch price was planned.

price_points.label: A/B test and selected presale price
Planned full price on launch day

pricing.notes: Koerner described the $97 presale as 67% off the planned $291 price. He later chose $97 after testing $47 and $97. The offer was described as lifetime and non-recurring.

acquisition_channels.details: Emailed active subscribers from Koerner's newsletter. He randomized the list, tagged and segmented test groups, excluded unsubscribed subscribers and people who had already received the test emails, and sent the winning offer to the remaining list.

quote.text: I'm going to take a sample of my entire email list and launch not just like test, but launch the business with a Stripe link to pay uh at one price to sample A and then at another price to sample B.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: The video explains the offer and directs viewers to a special link in its description or pinned comment.

quote.text: Also, by the way, if you're watching this, I've got a special link in the description where you can get lower price.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: Initially, the Stripe payment link redirected buyers to a Google Drive folder. Koerner later had his business partner download and organize the files into a Skool community, then invited buyers. He also recorded Loom videos, including a welcome walkthrough and a video showing the charity donation.
unit_economics_claims: Koerner reported $8,300 in revenue after 111 transactions and said costs were almost all profit, aside from Stripe transaction fees.
He later reported $23,000 in nearly pure profit after the full-list email and prior price tests.
He said total net profit across the video was between $30,000 and $40,000.
tools: Beehiiv for the newsletter, subscriber segments, tags, and email campaigns
Google Sheets for randomizing and dividing the email list
Stripe for one-time payment links, transaction analytics, and payment processing
Google Drive for hosting the original training materials
Skool for organizing the content and community
Loom for welcome and donation videos
Claude for reviewing A/B test results and creating a logo
ChatGPT for generating the community description
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated. Koerner bought the domain for $11.28 per year during setup; other setup costs were not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Koerner says the first $97 sale arrived in under two hours from the idea. He reports sending the first test email at about 12:30 and getting the first sale at 12:41.

acquisition.how: An opted-in newsletter can be segmented, emailed, and measured with software. UK marketing rules still require a valid basis to email subscribers and functioning unsubscribe handling.

onboarding.how: Stripe can take payment and redirect buyers to the materials; tagging and invitations can be automated. The transcript describes manual setup and some manual community invitations.

delivery.how: Digital files and recorded training can be delivered automatically. New material, AMAs, and community upkeep still require human work.

billing.how: Stripe payment links can collect one-time payments without manual invoicing. Refunds and exceptions may need a human.

support.how: A digital library can answer routine questions, but promised AMAs, community discussion, and refund requests need human involvement.

uk_applicability.notes: Digital training, email sales to an appropriately opted-in list, and online payment work in the UK. The founder would need to follow UK consumer, privacy, and email-marketing rules and make the offer's lifetime and support terms clear.

risks: The offer relies on an existing audience and trust; results may not transfer to a founder without a newsletter or established reputation.
A lifetime-content promise and 12 AMAs create ongoing delivery and support obligations.
The video presents short-term A/B results from a finite list; delayed purchases changed the relative results over time.
Email marketing in the UK requires an appropriate legal basis, accurate subscriber records, and working unsubscribe handling.
The host calls the product almost pure profit, but support, platform fees, refunds, and ongoing content work can reduce margins.
